common_name: Lucile Holley Louisiana Iris (Historic Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun; give it room, since this historic cultivar multiplies vigorously once established.

directions: Lucile Holley is a mid-20th-century Louisiana iris bred by hybridizer Charles W. Arny Jr., valued today mainly as an influential breeding parent behind later introductions, most notably Arny's own award-winning Easter Tide. Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun, where the rhizomes multiply readily along pond margins, ditch banks, and other spots that stay damp through summer. Give clumps room to spread and divide every three to four years in late summer to keep bloom vigorous. Its place in the pedigree of several modern Louisiana iris lines makes it an interesting historical addition to a collector's iris bed.

common_name: Blue Girl Holly (Meserve Hybrid Blue Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; plant a compatible male such as Blue Boy or Blue Prince nearby, since female and needs cross-pollination to set berries.

directions: Blue Girl is one of Kathleen Meserve's original blue holly hybrids, crossing English holly with the East Asian species Ilex rugosa to combine glossy, spiny, blue-green foliage with far greater winter hardiness than English holly alone. As a female selection it sets no fruit on its own but produces a heavy crop of bright red berries once pollinated by a nearby male such as Blue Boy or Blue Prince. Its dense, rounded, pyramidal habit holds up as a specimen, foundation planting, or informal hedge through winters that damage less hardy broadleaf evergreens. Plant one male for every three to five Blue-series females and give it the same acidic, well-drained soil other hollies prefer.

common_name: Apollo Winterberry Holly (Late Male Pollinator for Sparkleberry and Winter Red)

planting.note: Plant as a pollinator alongside late-blooming female cultivars such as Sparkleberry or Winter Red, positioning it centrally so a single male can service several nearby females.

directions: Apollo is a U.S. National Arboretum introduction bred by crossing native winterberry with the Japanese species Ilex serrata, selected specifically as a late-flowering male to pollinate late female winterberry cultivars such as Sparkleberry and Winter Red. It sets no berries of its own, but its inconspicuous spring flowers time closely with these late-blooming females, and its new foliage emerges flushed burgundy-red before settling to green through the growing season. A single vigorous plant can pollinate several females planted within range, so site it centrally among the group it serves. Prune only lightly right after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's wood.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun for the strongest bloom and rhizome increase.

directions: Valera is a Louisiana iris registered by hybridizer Charles W. Arny Jr. in 1980, bearing lightly ruffled apricot-buff flowers marked with a deep yellow signal line above pale green style arms. It later became a breeding parent in its own right, appearing in the pedigree of subsequent introductions such as Dorman Haymon's Praline Festival. Grow it in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting it at a pond margin or other low spot that stays damp. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in late summer to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Rose Of Abbeville Louisiana Iris (Historic Dormon-Bred Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, siting it at a pond margin or other low spot that stays damp through the growing season.

directions: Rose Of Abbeville was registered in 1949 by Louisiana naturalist and iris hybridizer Caroline Dormon, bred from the cross Old Coral x Peggy Mac and drawing on the wild Abbeville Reds that early Louisiana iris breeders prized for their rich color. It later proved influential as a breeding parent, most notably behind Dormon's own Wheelhorse, which went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award. Plant rhizome divisions in full sun in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil, where clumps multiply readily in a damp border or pond margin. Divide congested plantings every three to four years in late summer to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Violet Ray Louisiana Iris (Historic Pansy-Purple Dormon Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in consistently wet to moist, fertile soil in full sun, where rhizomes multiply readily into substantial clumps.

directions: Violet Ray was registered in 1949 by Caroline Dormon, bred from a large purple iris crossed with Old Coral, and bears broad, flat pansy-purple flowers brightened by a radiant light-yellow signal patch surrounded by cream rays. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1951 and the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1953, and later became a parent behind Dormon's influential Wheelhorse. Grow it in full sun in consistently wet to moist, fertile soil, where clumps expand quickly once established. Divide every three to four years in late summer to maintain strong bloom.

common_name: Caroline Gable Azalea (Late Red Gable Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade.

directions: Caroline Gable was bred by Pennsylvania hybridizer Joseph B. Gable, who named the selection for his daughter, and it flowers later in the season than most Gable hybrids, bearing red flowers marked with a deeper purple blotch. It shares the exceptional cold hardiness that made Gable's azaleas a breakthrough alternative to the tender Southern Indian hybrids popular in warmer regions, tolerating winter lows well below what many evergreen azaleas can survive. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it later served as a parent behind other Gable introductions, including the double-flowered Rosebud. Water deeply during dry spells, keep mulch over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set soon afterward.

common_name: New Horizon Bearded Iris (Historic 1946 Fay Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: New Horizon was registered by hybridizer Orville Fay in 1946 from the cross (Morocco Rose x a Hall seedling) x Overture, part of the same flamingo-pink breeding line that later produced several Dykes Medal winners. It bloomed very late in the bearded iris season and went on to serve as a parent behind Mary Randall, one of the most influential pink tall bearded irises of the mid-20th century. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun, and divide every three to four years after bloom to keep clumps vigorous. As a historic cultivar it is now mainly kept in circulation by historic iris preservation growers rather than mainstream retailers.

common_name: Pink Cameo Bearded Iris (Historic 1944 Fay Flamingo-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Pink Cameo was registered by Orville Fay in 1944 from the cross Seedling 42-02 x Overture, earning an Honorable Mention in 1946 and an Award of Merit in 1948 as part of Fay's pioneering flamingo-pink breeding line. It later became a parent behind Mary Randall, crossed with Cherie to produce the F2 pink seedling that, combined with New Horizon, gave rise to that American Dykes Medal winner. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained, full-sun soil, and divide every three to four years after bloom to keep the clump productive. Like other historic bearded iris introductions from this era, it survives today mainly in the collections of historic iris enthusiasts.
